newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH PREMIER UNVEILS RESCUE PLAN FOR GDANSK YARD.
newsitem.headline: POLISH PREMIER UNVEILS RESCUE PLAN FOR GDANSK YARD.

text.p: Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz on Thursday announced in parliament a rescue plan for the bankrupt Gdansk shipyard which if succesful could save 2,000 out of the yard's remaining 3,800 jobs.

Cimoszewicz said that under the plan the successful Szczecin shipyard would set up, with the use of the Gdansk yard's assets, a new subsidiary to build ships for Poland's PZM merchant shipping company.
"We have prepared together (with Szczecin shipyard and PZM) a plan of helping the (Gdansk) shipyard," Cimoszewicz said.
He said that under the plan the new company would build one ship for a German shipowner and complete one under construction, then build five vessels for PZM in 1998-2000.
"Such a plan allows the employment of about 2,000 workers including about 1,100 in production at the start of the project," Cimoszewicz said.
Cimoszewicz supported decisions by two Polish banks which had refused credits for the Gdansk yard to build five ships for the German owner, saying the contract was badly negotiated.
"Thanks to good the financial standing and sound management of Szczecin shipyard and the strong position of PZM...the chances of securing bank credits and government guarantees are bigger," he added.
He said that now the decisions rested with the Gdansk shipyard's receiver, who should hammer out the details of the new Szczecin-led venture.

The Solidarity trade union on Wednesday launched nationwide protests to halt the final collapse of the Gdansk shipyard and, after police forcibly ousted workers occupying three ministries in Warsaw, threatened to escalate their action.
The union accuses the coalition government, dominated by the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), of being motivated by political spite in letting the yard go under.

But Cimoszewicz said the shipyard fell victim to mismanagement and that his and previous governments have pumped enough taxpayers' money into the yard in futile attempts to help its turnaround. -- Tomasz Janowski +48 22 653 9700
